title: EXCLUSIVE: Law firm staff fear replacement by AI (RollOnFriday survey write-up + anonymous comment thread)
pub: RollOnFriday (reporting free-text responses to its Best Law Firms to Work At 2026 survey, with comment thread)
author: RollOnFriday; anonymous law-firm staff survey respondents and commenters

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: The anonymous thread contains no unified position. Several comments support the cluster’s emphasis on verification risks, value-based pricing and smaller production teams, while others predict sweeping lawyer replacement and inevitable firm contraction, going beyond the cluster’s bounded-automation and continuing-lawyer-value thesis. The claims are speculative and unsupported by systematic evidence.

We're going to automate the lot of you (and occasionally turn you off and back on again).

st.t: Law-firm pyramid: Efficiency threatens revenue and training
st.an: The source aligns with the cluster’s cautious position: AI output still requires expert supervision, while reported employment effects are limited to redundancies and staff perceptions rather than established evidence of broad AI-caused contraction. It provides anecdotal support for pressure on junior and business-staff roles without demonstrating profession-wide structural change.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source broadly supports the synthesis’s cautious, supervised-workflow framing: it emphasizes expert oversight and the risk of lawyers accepting AI research without verification. Although commenters predict redundancies and firm shrinkage, the article presents these as divided, anecdotal or unverified views rather than evidence of profession-wide replacement.

st.t: Task substitution: Complementarity can still reshape staffing
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s central proposition by pairing possible AI-related staffing changes with continued need for expert supervision. Its evidence is mainly conflicting staff perceptions, anonymous predictions and anecdotal tool complaints, so it reinforces the cluster’s caution that neither displacement nor performance claims are established causally.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source’s contrasting staff reports broadly support selective, human-supervised deployment: they describe current capability failures and substantial verification burdens while also identifying useful bounded applications and possible efficiency gains. Its displacement claims are largely uncorroborated staff predictions, consistent with the cluster’s conclusion that labour effects remain unsettled rather than demonstrating wholesale lawyer replacement.

kp.k: Survey responses reveal mixed attitudes toward AI adoption
kp.d: RollOnFriday reports AI-related free-text responses from its ongoing Best Law Firms to Work At 2026 survey, which had over 2,000 respondents so far. Selected responses include a White & Case staff member describing excessive enthusiasm for AI and a TLT trainee expressing fatigue with management's emphasis on it. The article supplies individual reactions rather than a quantified measure of how widespread these views are.
qs: with over 2,000 respondents having had their say about their firms - so far.
A hot topic emerging this year is the extent to which firms are encouraging their staff to use AI.
worryingly obsessed with AI

kp.k: Shoosmiths links staff bonuses to Copilot usage
kp.d: The article reports that Shoosmiths announced an extra £1million staff bonus pot conditional on collectively making one million Microsoft Copilot prompts. A lawyer at the firm defended the initiative as potentially leading over time to adoption of more suitable AI tools, rather than claiming that the current tools already met the firm's needs.
qs: it would provide an extra bonus pot of £1million to staff if they collectively made one million 'prompts' on Microsoft Copilot.
lead to the adoption of better, more suitable AI tools

kp.k: Staff connect redundancy processes with AI investment
kp.d: Freshfields reportedly cited a changing market and technology investment when commencing a redundancy process affecting paralegals; the article says many interpreted this as AI investment. A Freshfields staff member linked technology to worse culture and replacement of departing lawyers. Separately, a BCLP staff member attributed business staff redundancies that year to AI, while a Baker McKenzie business services employee expressed concern about surviving generative AI. These are reported firm explanations and staff interpretations, not an established causal finding that AI caused the redundancies.
qs: a fast-changing legal market
investing in technology
they can be replaced by AI
were because of AI
surviving the GEN AI revolution.

kp.k: AI adoption also attracts internal support
kp.d: A different BCLP employee expressed enthusiasm for a hoped-for organisational turnaround encompassing AI, innovation, growth markets and investment in people. This contrasts with the redundancy concerns expressed by another employee and presents AI as part of a growth narrative rather than solely a replacement strategy.
qs: excited by the opportunity to change BCLP's narrative to one that has steadied the ship, is embracing technology and innovation - especially AI - throughout the organization, is investing in growth markets and people, and is living up to the standard it has set as a full-service global firm

kp.k: Harvey trial feedback describes limitations and verification fatigue
kp.d: An anonymous US-firm associate criticised Harvey and relayed feedback from their firm's trial: difficulty with lengthy interactions, crashes when too many items were uploaded simultaneously, incomplete PDF word recognition, calculation limitations and fatigue among human checkers. These are anecdotal product criticisms, with no trial sample, protocol or measured error rates supplied.
qs: it is essentially ChatGPT in a legal wrapper, but somehow does our job worse
can't handle lengthy interactions
Other supposed shortfalls included an inability to recognise all words in a pdf, or to do calculations, and the infliction of "inaccuracy fatigue" on its human checkers.

kp.k: Supervision concerns accompany predictions of major AI failures
kp.d: The article stresses continuing expert supervision and reports an SRA warning against reliance on machine learning. In the anonymous thread, captured 2026-08-29, a commenter predicts that a major firm's generative-AI error will reverse some adoption and reports observing uncritical acceptance of AI research outputs even at leading firms. The anticipated failure and rollback are predictions, distinct from the article's references to existing misuse incidents.
qs: expert supervision
the SRA has warned lawyers
not to rely
I’m predicting that sooner than we think, one major law firm is going to have a gigantic cock-up caused by Gen AI. It will roll back a lot of this.
Even at the top firms it shocks me how often people just instantly believe whatever the AI tool spits out when they’re doing research.

kp.k: Commenters foresee adoption becoming workforce substitution
kp.d: One anonymous commenter asserts that firms encourage AI engagement to create datasets enabling replacement of most staff within a few years. Interpreting a quoted statement about DWF's use of Legora for volume operations, contracts and time-intensive tasks, the commenter predicts replacement of most staff in the affected teams within eighteen months. Another predicts smaller firms because legal work has become increasingly process-based over the last 20 years. These are commenters' proposed mechanisms and forecasts, not reported workforce outcomes.
qs: At the end of the day we know our firms are encouraging staff to engage with AI in order to build up a dataset which means most of the staff are replaceable in a few years.
DWF will use Legora to streamline its volume-based legal operations, manage contracts and automate time-intensive tasks, benefiting fully from the deep capabilities of the platform
DWF will be using Legora instead of most of the staff in those teams in eighteen months.
the solicitors profession has spent the last 20 years process-ising everything they do, and where you have a process, you will land up with a machine that can do it better.
Law firms will reduce in size, that is inevitable at this stage.

kp.k: Replacement fears may undermine retention, quality and client relationships
kp.d: An anonymous commenter proposes a deteriorating cycle: staff leave when they believe they are training their replacements, weaker recruits supply poorer AI training material, and clients subsequently seek the experts they previously used. The commenter alleges Shoosmiths, Beachcroft and DWF already face this problem. A reply questions whether staff can escape AI-related efficiency efforts by changing firms. These claims are not supported with retention or client-loss data in the document.
qs: Once they know they’re training a computer to replace them, they leave.
They’re then replaced by poorer staff and the AI is trained upon a product that doesn’t match what you offered.
The firm is left with a lower cost base but also loses clients.
Firms like Shoosmiths, Beachcroft and DWF are facing this problem at the moment.
Is there any firm that isn't seeking "AI-related efficiencies" in some way?

kp.k: Comments connect substitution with pricing and specific tasks
kp.d: One commenter couples anticipated displacement of junior and mid-level lawyers with a demand for value-billing proposals, without specifying a pricing model. Another claims offshore lawyers could be replaced because their work consists of forwarding and filing onshore lawyers' material. A further commenter conditionally welcomes AI producing satisfactory instructions and bundles for counsel. These are informal opinions about substitution and task utility, not demonstrated capabilities.
qs: AI is the future and snotty nosed junior and mid level lawyers are out. Now let's see your value billing proposals.
You could easily replace offshore lawyers with AI, given that their sole function is to be a post box for onshore lawyers and simply file what is sent to them.
If AI produces decent instructions and bundles for counsel, bring it on.

kp.k: Litigation authority prompts conflicting anonymous legal interpretations
kp.d: One commenter invokes Mazur to question whether AI could conduct litigation if paralegals cannot. Another disputes that interpretation and asserts that a qualified person's signature suffices. The thread raises the boundary between automation, nonlawyer work and qualified-lawyer responsibility, but supplies no legal analysis resolving these conflicting assertions.
qs: Mazur says paralegals can’t conduct litigation. Can AI ??
Mazur does not say that. As long as a qualified person signs things it's all fine ...

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The source presents competing claims about AI adoption, replacement of staff, service quality, verification burdens and changes to law-firm economics.
pts.d: RollOnFriday reports that firms are encouraging AI use, including Shoosmiths' offer of an additional £1 million bonus pool if staff collectively make one million Microsoft Copilot prompts. A Shoosmiths lawyer predicts this will eventually encourage adoption of more suitable tools. The article says expert supervision remains necessary and reports an SRA warning against reliance on machine learning. On employment, the article reports Freshfields' paralegal redundancy process and its stated investment in technology, but identifies the AI explanation as an interpretation rather than an explicit firm confirmation. A Freshfields staffer associates technological change with deteriorating culture and lawyers leaving because they can be replaced by AI. A BCLP staffer attributes business staff redundancies to AI; another BCLP respondent instead welcomes AI as part of innovation, growth and investment in people. A Baker McKenzie business services respondent expresses concern about surviving generative AI rather than a specific displacement forecast. An associate at an unnamed US firm reports shortcomings in Harvey, including difficulties with lengthy interactions, crashes when too many items are uploaded, PDF word recognition, calculations and fatigue among human verifiers. In the anonymous comments, one contributor predicts that staff engagement builds a dataset enabling widespread replacement within a few years and specifically predicts that Legora will replace most staff in certain DWF teams within eighteen months. Another forecasts a major firm's serious generative-AI error and a consequent retreat from adoption. A further commenter predicts a chain of departures, poorer replacement staff, degraded AI training material, loss of expertise and client losses, and claims Shoosmiths, Beachcroft and DWF already face this problem. Another argues that process-based legal work will be performed better by machines and that firms will inevitably shrink. Other comments advocate removing junior and mid-level lawyers while asking for value-billing proposals, claim offshore lawyers could readily be replaced, or conditionally welcome AI-generated instructions and bundles for counsel. A self-identified Legal IT worker's prediction of wholesale automation is presented humorously, not as a documented implementation plan.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists mainly of selected anonymous survey responses and comments, reported firm initiatives and redundancy announcements, and linked regulatory or incident reporting—not measured displacement or performance results.
pts.d: RollOnFriday states that its ongoing Best Law Firms to Work At 2026 survey has more than 2,000 respondents, but supplies no AI-specific response counts, sampling methodology or quantitative estimate of the prevalence of these views. The anonymous comments and their vote totals are not a representative survey of AI's effects. The Shoosmiths incentive is a reported initiative, not evidence that better tools have subsequently been adopted. Freshfields' stated reasons reference market change and technology; the specific link to AI is attributed to interpretations and staff comments. The BCLP redundancy explanation is one staffer's attribution without corroborating causal evidence in the supplied text. The Harvey claims are an associate's account of feedback from a firm trial, not a benchmark, direct transcript of testing, or quantified error study. RollOnFriday links to reports concerning expert supervision, an SRA warning and AI-related misconduct or misuse; the underlying sources are not reproduced here. The DWF replacement prediction is a commenter's interpretation of a quoted statement about streamlining operations with Legora, not a DWF announcement of staff replacement. The predicted major failure is supported by the commenter's stated observation that lawyers readily trust AI research output. The predicted staff-quality-client-loss cycle and claims about offshore replacement and inevitable firm shrinkage offer assertions and causal reasoning rather than documented outcomes. The Legal IT commenter invokes occupational experience but frames wholesale automation as a joke. The comments about Mazur are conflicting legal assertions or questions, not demonstrated AI capabilities or a settled statement of the law.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Claims range from present experiences to explicit replacement forecasts of eighteen months or a few years; most other predictions have no fixed deadline.
pts.d: The supplied metadata identifies the article as 2025 reporting on the ongoing 2026 survey and separately dates capture of the comment thread to 2026-08-29. Individual comment dates are not supplied, so relative predictions should not be converted into calendar deadlines. Shoosmiths' anticipated improvement in tool adoption is qualified by 'in time', and the bonus depends on collectively reaching one million Copilot prompts. Freshfields' redundancy process is described as recent; BCLP redundancies are described as occurring 'this year'. The Harvey problems are presented as feedback from a trial, without dates, model versions or testing conditions. The dataset-and-replacement commenter predicts broad replaceability 'in a few years' and replacement of most staff in the specified DWF teams 'in eighteen months'. The predicted major AI failure will occur 'sooner than we think', with retrenchment conditional on that incident. The staff departure and client-loss scenario unfolds 'over time' and depends on staff believing they are training their replacements, inferior successors and clients seeking lost expertise. The shrinkage prediction rests on the premise that process-based work can be performed better by machines. Support for AI-produced counsel materials explicitly depends on their being decent. No definite adoption deadline accompanies the offshore replacement claim, the value-billing demand or the humorous wholesale-automation forecast.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are law-firm employees, lawyers verifying AI work, process-heavy teams and firms' clients; the document does not substantiate wider access-to-justice effects.
pts.d: Freshfields paralegals face a reported redundancy process, while a staffer also describes lawyers leaving amid perceived AI replaceability. BCLP business staff are the subjects of a respondent's AI-related redundancy allegation, and a Baker McKenzie business services employee voices job-security anxiety. Shoosmiths staff are incentivised to use Copilot. A White & Case staffer and a TLT trainee report dissatisfaction with management's emphasis on AI, indicating cultural effects without establishing displacement. The unnamed US firm's associate and human checkers face allegedly unreliable Harvey output and verification fatigue. The DWF forecast concerns teams doing volume-based legal operations, contract management and time-intensive tasks, rather than a demonstrated reduction across the whole firm. Other anonymous commenters target junior and mid-level lawyers, offshore lawyers and staff performing process-based work for potential substitution. The expertise-loss scenario affects departing employees, replacement staff, clients seeking expert advice and firms whose cost savings may be offset by lost clients. The major-error prediction includes leading firms and their research practices. Counsel are possible beneficiaries of useful AI-prepared instructions and bundles. Partners appear in satire and in a request for changed pricing, not in an evidenced finding that their jobs are protected. No concrete claim establishes benefits for unmet civil legal need or the public generally.
